stages.title: Cell structures and functions
stages.hook: An animal cell and a leaf cell are both alive, yet a leaf cell is green and box-shaped. What extra parts does it have, and what do they do?
explain: Cells contain organelles, small structures with specific jobs. The nucleus holds the DNA and controls the cell. The cytoplasm is the jelly where many reactions happen. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration. Ribosomes build proteins.

Plant cells also have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose, a large vacuole filled with cell sap that keeps the cell firm, and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis. Bacterial cells are prokaryotes: they have no nucleus, and their DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm.

Cells are measured in micrometres (µm), where 1 mm = 1000 µm. A light microscope shows cells; an electron microscope shows much finer detail, such as ribosomes. Magnification = image size ÷ real size.

example.q: A cell is drawn 60 mm wide. Its real width is 0.03 mm. What is the magnification?
steps: Use magnification = image size ÷ real size.

analogies.city: The nucleus is city hall, mitochondria are power stations, the membrane is the border control.
analogies.home: A house has a thermostat (nucleus), a boiler (mitochondria) and doors with locks (membrane).
analogies.tech: Ribosomes are like 3D printers that assemble proteins from instructions.

stages.mnemonic: Nucleus directs, Mitochondria Make energy, Ribosomes build, Membrane guards.
terms: A small structure inside a cell with a specific job.

misc.right: Plant cells have both. They respire in mitochondria all the time and photosynthesise in chloroplasts in the light.

stages.title: Biological molecules
stages.hook: Bread, butter and egg white all feed you, but they are made of very different chemicals. What are they?
explain: Living things are built from carbon-based molecules. Carbohydrates (sugars, starch) give energy. Lipids (fats and oils) store energy and form membranes. Proteins build and repair tissues and act as enzymes. Nucleic acids (DNA) store genetic information. Water and minerals are also needed.

Many large molecules are polymers made of small units: starch is made of glucose units, proteins of amino acids, and fats of fatty acids and glycerol. Digestion breaks them back into small units that can be absorbed.

Food tests identify them. Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch. Benedict's solution turns from blue to green, yellow or brick-red when heated with reducing sugars. Biuret reagent turns purple with protein. Ethanol then water gives a cloudy white emulsion with lipids.

example.q: A food turns iodine solution blue-black. What does it contain?
steps: Iodine is the test for starch.

teach.model: Carbohydrates give energy, lipids store energy, proteins build and repair, and DNA stores genetic information. Big molecules are made of small units: starch from glucose, proteins from amino acids.

stages.title: Cell membranes and transport
stages.hook: Leave a piece of potato in salty water and it shrinks. Leave it in pure water and it gets firm. Why?
explain: The cell membrane is partially permeable: it lets some substances through but not others. It is made of a double layer of lipids with proteins embedded. Substances cross the membrane in three main ways.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, down a concentration gradient. It needs no energy. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane, from dilute solution to concentrated solution. Active transport moves substances against a gradient, from low to high concentration, and it uses energy from respiration.
Surface area to volume ratio matters. Small cells have a bigger ratio than large ones, so materials can reach all parts of the cell quickly.

example.q: A cube cell has sides of 2 cm. Find the surface area to volume ratio.

analogies.home: A door that lets in only family members is like a membrane.
analogies.farm: Plants take in minerals from soil even when the soil has less of them: active transport.
analogies.city: A crowd spreads out from a packed stadium into empty streets as diffusion does.

stages.mnemonic: Diffusion rolls down the hill (free), active transport pushes up the hill (needs energy).
terms: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
Diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane.
Movement against a concentration gradient using energy.
A difference in concentration between two regions.

misc.wrong: In osmosis, the solute moves through the membrane.
misc.right: In osmosis it is water that moves, from the dilute side to the more concentrated side.

teach.model: Diffusion is particles spreading from where there are lots to where there are few, with no energy needed. Osmosis is the same for water through a membrane. Active transport moves substances the other way, from few to many, so it needs energy.

stages.title: Cellular respiration
stages.hook: Your muscles keep working for hours on food, but a sprinter's legs burn after seconds. What are cells doing differently?
explain: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose in cells, mainly in mitochondria. Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). Symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. The energy is used to make ATP, the cell's energy currency.

Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen and releases much less energy. In muscles, glucose → lactic acid. In yeast, glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, which is how bread rises and drinks ferment. The build-up of lactic acid is linked to muscle fatigue, and extra oxygen is needed afterwards (oxygen debt) to break it down.
Respiration is controlled by enzymes, so it speeds up with warmth, but very high temperatures damage enzymes.

example.q: How many CO₂ molecules are made when 3 glucose molecules respire aerobically?

analogies.sport: A marathon runner runs aerobically; a 100 m sprinter relies more on quick anaerobic energy.
analogies.farm: Brewing and baking use yeast respiring without oxygen.
analogies.tech: ATP is like a rechargeable battery, repeatedly charged and discharged.

stages.mnemonic: Aerobic = Air in, big payoff. Anaerobic = no air, small payoff.
terms: Releasing energy from glucose using oxygen.
Molecule that carries usable energy in cells.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast making ethanol and CO₂.

misc.wrong: Respiration is another word for breathing.
misc.right: Breathing moves gases; respiration is the chemical process in cells that releases energy.

stages.limits: Real cells make about 30 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration, and the exact number varies by conditions, so textbook values differ.

stages.title: Genetics fundamentals
stages.hook: Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child, yet two blue-eyed parents rarely have a brown-eyed child. How can traits skip a generation?
explain: Genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits. We inherit one set of chromosomes from each parent, so for most genes we have two alleles (versions). An allele can be dominant (shows even if only one copy is present) or recessive (shows only if both copies are recessive).

Genotype is the pair of alleles; phenotype is the visible trait. A person with two identical alleles is homozygous; with two different alleles, heterozygous. Gregor Mendel found these patterns by breeding pea plants in the 1860s.

A Punnett square shows possible offspring. Cross two heterozygotes (Tt × Tt): the offspring are 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 show the dominant trait and 1 the recessive: a 3:1 ratio, or 25% recessive. These are probabilities for each child, not guarantees.

example.q: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). Cross Tt × Tt. What percentage are short?
steps: Gametes from each parent: T or t.
Only tt is short: 1 out of 4.

analogies.home: Recipe cards: you get one from each parent, and one may be louder than the other.
analogies.farm: Breeders track coat colour in cattle using these patterns.
analogies.music: Two instruments play a note; a loud one (dominant) hides the quiet one (recessive).

stages.mnemonic: Big letter shows (dominant); little letter hides unless it has a twin.

misc.wrong: A dominant allele is always the most common one.
misc.right: Dominant means it shows when present; it does not mean common. Some dominant alleles are rare.

stages.limits: Many traits, like height, are controlled by several genes and the environment, so simple dominant-recessive patterns are only a starting model.

trip.prompt: Find Mendel's pea plant experiment. What ratio did he find in the second generation?

teach.topic: How a Punnett square predicts offspring
teach.model: A Punnett square lists the alleles each parent can pass on and shows every combination. If both parents are Tt, the offspring are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. So one in four, or 25%, are tt. It gives probabilities, not certainties.

What does the result tell you?

stages.title: Human organ systems
stages.hook: When you stand up quickly, your heart rate jumps within seconds. What sends the message so fast?
explain: Organ systems cooperate. The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients. The circulatory system pumps blood through the heart, arteries, capillaries and veins to carry oxygen and nutrients. The respiratory system exchanges gases in the lungs. The nervous system and endocrine system (hormones) coordinate the body. The excretory system, including the kidneys, removes waste.

Blood has red cells (carry oxygen using haemoglobin), white cells (fight infection), platelets (clot) and plasma (the liquid). The heart has four chambers, and the blood goes round twice in a double circulation: heart to lungs and back, then heart to body and back.
The kidneys filter blood, remove urea and control water balance. This is part of homeostasis, keeping conditions inside the body steady.

example.q: Trace the path of blood from the body back to the lungs.
steps: Deoxygenated blood returns from the body to the right atrium.
It passes to the right ventricle.
It is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
example.a: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs.

Blood goes slower and so loses less oxygen

It needs no heart to push the blood around
panel.why: The heart boosts the blood pressure again after the lungs.

teach.topic: How the circulatory system delivers oxygen
teach.model: The lungs add oxygen to the blood. The heart pumps the blood through arteries to the body. Red blood cells carry the oxygen, and capillaries let it pass into cells. Veins bring the blood back to the heart.

stages.title: Plant physiology
stages.hook: A tall tree lifts hundreds of litres of water to its top leaves each day with no pump. What pulls it up?
explain: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata. As water evaporates, it pulls more water up the xylem from the roots, like drinking through a straw. This transpiration stream carries water and dissolved minerals. Water is also needed for photosynthesis and keeps cells firm.

Guard cells open and close the stomata. They let carbon dioxide in but allow water to escape, so plants balance gas exchange and water loss. Transpiration is faster when it is hot, dry, windy and bright.

Phloem moves sugars from leaves to growing parts and stores (translocation). Plants also respond to stimuli: shoots grow towards light (phototropism) and away from gravity, roots grow down (gravitropism). Hormones called auxins control this.

example.q: Why does transpiration speed up on a hot, windy day?
steps: Heat gives water molecules more energy to evaporate.
Wind carries away vapour near the leaf, keeping the gradient steep.
example.a: Heat and wind increase evaporation from the leaf.

analogies.home: Wet laundry dries faster in warm wind.
analogies.farm: Crops need more irrigation in hot, dry weather.
analogies.nature: Desert plants have small leaves to reduce water loss.

stages.mnemonic: Xylem pulls water up; phloem sends sugar around; stomata are the doors.
terms: Loss of water vapour from leaves.
Pores in leaves for gas exchange.

misc.wrong: Plants have no hormones because they have no nervous system.
misc.right: Plants use hormones such as auxin to coordinate growth and responses.

trip.prompt: Find a diagram of the transpiration stream. Trace one water molecule from soil to air.

questions.q: Which cells control the opening of stomata?

Red blood cells
Palisade cells

questions.q: What is transpiration?

Making sugar in the leaf cells

teach.topic: What transpiration is and why it matters
teach.model: Water evaporates from the leaves through stomata. This pulls more water up the stem from the roots, carrying minerals with it. Hot, dry or windy weather makes it faster. It lets the plant take in carbon dioxide but also risks losing water.

points.ask: What does it do for the plant?

stages.title: Microorganisms
stages.hook: Yogurt, bread and some diseases all come from tiny living things you cannot see. How can the same group be helpful and harmful?
explain: Microorganisms are living things too small to see with the naked eye. The main groups are bacteria (single-celled, no nucleus), viruses (tiny particles that reproduce only inside host cells), fungi such as yeast and mould, and protists such as amoeba.

Many are helpful: bacteria make yogurt and cheese, yeast makes bread rise, decomposers recycle nutrients, and gut bacteria help digestion. Some cause disease, called pathogens: bacteria cause tetanus, viruses cause flu, and a protist causes malaria. Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work on viruses.
Bacteria can multiply fast by binary fission. If one divides every 20 minutes, the number doubles each time. Vaccines, clean water, handwashing and cooking food reduce the spread of disease.

example.q: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria after 2 hours?

analogies.home: Handwashing clears away germs as washing dishes clears away food scraps.
analogies.farm: Farmers use bacteria to make yogurt and fungi to make some cheeses.
analogies.city: Water treatment plants clean drinking water to remove pathogens.

stages.mnemonic: Bacteria = Beneficial or Bad; Viruses need a Victim cell.
terms: A single-celled organism with no nucleus.
A tiny particle that reproduces only inside host cells.

misc.right: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria.

stages.limits: Whether viruses count as living is debated, because they cannot reproduce on their own.

teach.topic: Why some microorganisms are helpful and others harmful
teach.model: Microorganisms are tiny living things such as bacteria, fungi and protists, plus viruses. Many are helpful: yeast makes bread and bacteria make yogurt. Some are pathogens and cause disease. Good hygiene and vaccines help prevent illness.

points.ask: How can they harm us, and what can we do?

stages.title: Evolution and adaptation
stages.hook: Fossils show that whales once had legs. How could a land animal's descendants end up living in the sea?
explain: Evolution is the change in the inherited features of populations over many generations. The scientific consensus, supported by fossils, DNA and observed changes, is that all living things share common ancestors and that species change over time.

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace explained how: natural selection. Individuals in a population vary. Some variations help survival and reproduction in their environment. Those individuals leave more offspring, passing on the helpful alleles, so over generations the helpful feature becomes more common.

An adaptation is a feature that helps an organism survive in its habitat, such as a camel's fat store in its hump, or thick fur on a polar bear. Variation comes from mutations and from mixing genes in reproduction. Species that cannot adapt to a fast change may go extinct.

example.q: In a field, dark moths are hidden on dark tree bark but pale moths are easily seen by birds. After many years, what is likely?
steps: Birds eat more of the pale moths.
More dark moths survive and breed.

analogies.nature: Giraffes with slightly longer necks reached more leaves and more of their young survived over many generations.
analogies.farm: Farmers choose the biggest cobs for seed, which is artificial selection and shows how repeated choices change a population.
analogies.sea: Fish in dark caves lose their colour and sight over generations because these are not helpful there.

terms: Change in inherited features of a population over generations.
Individuals with helpful features survive and reproduce more.
A feature that helps survival in a habitat.

misc.wrong: Individuals change during their lives to suit the environment, and pass those changes on.
misc.right: Populations change, not individuals. Selection acts on inherited variation that was already there.

The helpful feature becomes more common

questions.q: In a population of 200 moths, 150 are dark. What percentage are dark?

questions.q: Explain how natural selection could make a population of beetles more green over time if green beetles are harder for birds to see.

questions.why: Selection plus inheritance produces change.

questions.q: Fossils of simple fish are found in older rock layers and fossils of land animals in younger layers. What does this suggest?

panel.q: Which of these provides evidence for evolution?

A person's opinion about how animals first began
A favourite story told by village elders long ago
The colour of the sky at sunset on a clear day

panel.q: A mutation creates a new allele. When can natural selection act on it?
o: If it affects survival or reproduction
Never
Only in plants

panel.why: Selection acts when alleles change fitness.

panel.q: A scientist says, 'Evolution is just a theory.' Which reply is best?
o: In science a theory is a well-tested explanation supported by lots of evidence
A scientific theory means only a guess made by one person without checking
It is a belief that cannot be checked by anyone, so ignore it
Theories in science cannot be tested by any experiment or observation
panel.why: A scientific theory is a tested explanation, not a guess.

teach.model: Individuals in a population differ. Those with features that help them survive have more offspring and pass on their alleles. Over many generations that feature becomes more common. So populations adapt, not single individuals.

points.ask: What do individuals in a population have?
